sections.title: The Kashrut of Milk
sections.html:
Pure milk is milk that was milked from a pure (kosher) domesticated or wild animal, that is, from species of domesticated and wild animals whose meat is kosher to eat, such as a cow, a goat and a deer. Impure milk is milk that was milked from an impure domesticated or wild animal, whose meat is forbidden to eat, such as a she-donkey, a female camel, a mare and a sow. This is the rule: "That which comes from the impure is impure, and that which comes from the pure is pure" (Bekhorot 5b).1

There are two differences between pure and impure milk: a) Pure milk can curdle into cheese, whereas impure milk does not curdle. b) The color of pure milk is white, and that of impure milk is yellowish (Avoda Zara 35b).

Even when the milk is pure, it may still be forbidden, for if it was milked from a tereifa animal, it is forbidden to eat. A tereifa is an animal that was injured in a way that it will not live more than twelve months, or that has another defect that will cause its death within twelve months (above 20:2). Since death is eating away at its flesh, even if it is slaughtered with a kosher sheḥita, its meat is forbidden to eat. And since its meat is forbidden to eat, its milk is also forbidden to eat. If a tereifa animal became mixed in with kosher animals and was milked together with the other animals, then if the kosher animals were sixty times the tereifa, the milk of the tereifa is nullified in sixty and all the milk milked from the herd is kosher; and if they were not sixty times as many, all the milk is forbidden (SA YD 81:1-2).

If a cow was milked and afterwards slaughtered, and it turned out to be a tereifa, just as its meat is forbidden to eat, so the milk that was milked from it is forbidden to eat, and the cheese made from that milk is also forbidden to eat. But if it is possible that the defect that rendered it tereifa arose after the milk from which the cheese was made was milked from it, the cheese is kosher, for as long as there is no proof that the animal was a tereifa at the time of milking, its milk retains the presumptive status of being kosher (ibid.).

When an animal became tereifa because of a lung adhesion (sirkha), the milk that was milked from it in the three days closest to its slaughter is forbidden. However, milk that was milked from it before then is permitted because of a 'double doubt' (sfek sfeika): perhaps the adhesion formed after the milk was milked, and perhaps this adhesion does not render it tereifa (SA and Rema YD 81:2; Zivḥei Tzedek 18; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 27).2

sections.title: The Prohibition of Milk of Non-Jews (Ḥalav Akum)
sections.html:
The Sages forbade Jews to eat milk that a non-Jew milked, lest he mixed impure milk into the pure milk (Avoda Zara 35b). This is despite the fact that the likelihood of this is very small, since the overwhelming majority of the milk that people usually drink and eat is pure milk. Moreover, there is a difference between impure and pure milk, for the color of pure milk is white and the color of impure milk is yellowish; consequently, if the milk is white and no different taste is detected in it, then even if the non-Jew mixed impure milk into it, by Torah law it is nullified in the majority of pure milk. Nevertheless, the Sages were very stringent and forbade the milk of a non-Jew lest he mixed impure milk into it. Not only that, but even if a Jew made cheese from a non-Jew's milk, which would seem to prove that the milk is pure, since the milk of an impure animal does not curdle, the Sages forbade the cheese, out of concern that impure milk that did not curdle remained as moisture in the cavities and crevices of the cheese. Apparently, the Sages were more stringent about this concern of prohibition than is customary with other food prohibitions because of the general aim of distancing Jews from the foods of non-Jews.3

However, when a Jew supervises the non-Jew so that he does not mix impure milk into the pure milk, the milk is kosher. If it is known with certainty that the non-Jew has no impure animal, it is sufficient that the Jew watches that the non-Jew does not bring milk from elsewhere in the middle of the milking. If the non-Jew has an impure animal, the Jew must watch that he milks the pure animal and does not mix milk of the impure animal into its milk. He need not see the entire milking; rather, it is sufficient that the non-Jew knows that the Jew is supervising him and could easily see him, for example, if he stood up he would see him milking, or he could come in and see him at any moment (Avoda Zara 39b; SA 115:1). When there is a concern that impure milk remained in the non-Jew's vessel from a previous milking, the Jew must check that the vessel is clean of milk residue (Rema and commentators there).

sections.title: Milk of Non-Jews When There Is No Concern of Impure Milk
sections.html:
Three views have been stated regarding the scope of the prohibition. According to the first view, only when there is a realistic concern that the non-Jew will mix impure milk into the pure milk is milk milked by a non-Jew forbidden. But in a place where impure animals are not raised, or where the milk of an impure animal is much more expensive, there is no concern that the non-Jew will mix impure milk into pure, and a Jew may eat milk that a non-Jew milked (Tashbetz, Rashbash, Pri Ḥadash). And so was the custom in most communities of North Africa and Yemen.

According to the second view, even in a place where there is no realistic concern that the non-Jew will mix impure milk into pure, as long as there is any concern whatsoever, even an extremely remote one, a Jew may not eat milk that a non-Jew milked. In practice, since impure animals were sometimes brought from place to place, and sometimes the non-Jew thought he would benefit from mixing impure milk into the pure milk, in order to preserve it for a long time or to improve its taste, they forbade all milk milked by a non-Jew. Only when the non-Jew milked the pure animals in a place where there is no concern at all that impure milk will be brought to him is the milk kosher. And so was the custom in many communities in the regions around the Land of Israel and in Ashkenaz (Ḥida, Beit Meir, Ḥokhmat Adam).

According to the third view, even when there is no concern at all that the non-Jew will mix impure milk into pure, the milk milked by the non-Jew is forbidden. This is because, on the basis of the concern that the non-Jew might mix impure milk into pure, the Sages decreed by a vote (be-minyan), that is, by a definitive decision, a complete prohibition on the milk of non-Jews, even when there is no concern at all that impure milk is mixed into it (Ḥatam Sofer, Ḥelkat Ya'akov).4

sections.title: The Dispute about Milk from Large Companies Today
sections.html:
Many hold that since in practice there is no concern that the large companies that market milk and its products will mix impure milk into their milk, because impure animals are not milked for them at all, and the price of impure milk is incomparably higher than that of pure milk, and there is also no benefit in mixing it into pure milk, according to most poskim (the first and second views in the previous halakha) their milk is not subject to the prohibition of 'milk of non-Jews.' Rav Moshe Feinstein added (Igrot Moshe YD 1:47-49) that even according to the stringent view, one may be lenient regarding dairy products of reliable, supervised companies in well-ordered countries that declare that the milk and its products they market are the milk of pure animals. This is because if they deceive, they are liable to be fined, and no less seriously, consumer trust in their products is liable to be harmed, and they will lose many customers. It follows that the general supervision in these countries is considered like the supervision of a Jew who watches that impure milk is not mixed into the pure milk, and consequently, according to all views, their milk is permitted. Therefore, taking into account the difficulty of obtaining 'ḥalav Yisrael' (milk milked under Jewish supervision) outside Israel, Rav Feinstein permitted in the USA relying on the reliability of supervised companies. And this is the practice of the widespread kashrut system in the USA, the OU.

On the other hand, some are stringent, for two main reasons: a) Perhaps the government supervision is not tight enough, and even if it is tight, people might learn from this to be lenient in places that are not properly supervised. b) According to the view that the prohibition of milk of non-Jews is a complete prohibition enacted by a vote (the third view in the previous halakha), even if the government supervision is tight, it is not considered like the supervision of a Jew that the Sages permitted, and consequently the milk is forbidden (Ḥelkat Ya'akov YD 34; Mishneh Halakhot 4:103).

In practice, the main ruling follows the lenient opinion; however, the holy people of Israel are accustomed to be scrupulous when this does not involve great difficulty, as explained below (in halakha 6).

Today it is possible to supervise the milking by electronic means, and when this supervision is managed properly, the milk is kosher le-mehadrin according to all views.5

sections.title: Powdered Milk of Non-Jews
sections.html:
Another dispute arose regarding 'powdered milk,' that is, milk whose liquids have been evaporated until only a powder remains of it. 'Powdered milk' is used to flavor products such as chocolate, when the concentrated substances and flavors of milk are wanted without the added volume of the liquids. Also, 'powdered milk' can be stored for a long time, and when needed, water can be added to it to obtain a drink similar to regular milk, containing almost all its nutritional components.

According to most poskim, since it is clear to us that the 'powdered milk' was made from pure milk, according to the first and second views we learned in the previous halakhot, it is kosher. In addition, in well-ordered countries where the companies are supervised so that they do not deceive and introduce impure milk into the cow's milk from which 'powdered milk' is produced, the governmental and public supervision can be regarded as the supervision of a Jew, and then even according to the third view the milk would be kosher. And even one who does not agree to be lenient on the basis of these arguments regarding the milk of a non-Jew should be lenient regarding 'powdered milk,' because the Sages decreed a prohibition on milk milked by a non-Jew and not on a new product made from it. Just as they needed to enact an additional decree regarding cheese, and without it cheese would have been permitted, so too, without a special decree on 'powdered milk,' when it is clear to us that it was made from the milk of a pure animal, it is permitted to eat.

Some of those who are stringent regarding a non-Jew's milk milked for a reliable company are also stringent regarding 'powdered milk' made from it, because 'powdered milk' is the milk itself without its liquids, and consequently the decree on the milk of a non-Jew also applies to 'powdered milk' produced from it. And the reason a special decree had to be enacted regarding cheese is that cheese is always produced from pure milk, since only pure milk curdles, and consequently, when they wished to forbid the cheese of non-Jews, they had to forbid it by an additional decree for other reasons. But 'powdered milk' can also be made from impure milk, and consequently the decree on milk applies to it as well.6

sections.title: Practical Halakha Regarding Dairy Products
sections.html:
In the fundamental dispute about milk and 'powdered milk' from reliable, supervised companies, the halakha follows the lenient opinion, because their reasoning is convincing, and the opinion of most of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim is to be lenient; and in addition, the rule is that in a dispute concerning rabbinic law, the halakha follows the lenient opinion. Regarding 'powdered milk,' the position of those who permit is even broader, since even among those who are stringent regarding a non-Jew's milk there are some who are lenient regarding 'powdered milk.' Therefore, regular kashrut certification may be given to dairy products known not to contain impure milk, even though they were milked without Jewish supervision. However, mehadrin kashrut should be given only to milk milked under Jewish supervision, by a supervisor or by cameras. And the holy people of Israel, as long as the stringency does not involve high costs, are accustomed to be scrupulous in accordance with all the poskim. Therefore, in all the certifications of the rabbinates in the Land of Israel it is accepted practice to be scrupulous not to use milk of non-Jews, but products containing powdered milk are given certification according to the basic halakha.

Mehadrin kashrut requires care regarding two more issues. The first: as we learned (above 20:3), veterinarians sometimes have to perform operations on animals, such as a Caesarean section on an animal having difficulty giving birth, and perforating the rumen to release dangerous gases. Some say that after these operations they are considered tereifot, and consequently their milk becomes forbidden to eat. And although we learned (above 20, note 4) that the main halakhic ruling follows the lenient authorities, who hold that these operations do not render the cows tereifa, and in addition, the milk of the operated cows is nullified in the milk of the kosher ones, in mehadrin kashrut one should take into account the stringent opinion and not mix in milk from cows that underwent such operations.

The second: in mehadrin kashrut one must be careful not to mix in milk milked in dairy barns where Shabbat observance is not maintained. And indeed, as we will learn (in halakha 11), since the prohibition of benefiting from milk milked in desecration of Shabbat is rabbinic, in a situation of doubt there is no prohibition. Therefore, in regular kashrut it is possible to include milk brought from dairy barns where Shabbat observance is not maintained, since there is no certainty that it is milk milked in desecration of Shabbat, for perhaps it was milked on a weekday and perhaps it was milked on Shabbat by a non-Jew. But in mehadrin kashrut one must be careful to use milk from dairy barns where Shabbat observance is maintained.

In summary, kashrut certification may be given to milk of non-Jews, and to 'powdered milk' made from milk of non-Jews, that was milked for large, supervised companies, without concern about milk of tereifot. Likewise, kashrut certification may be given to milk from Jewish dairy barns where they are not careful to milk without desecrating Shabbat. And so various kashrut bodies practice. Those who wish to be scrupulous are stringent on these four issues, and this is the definition of dairy products that are kosher le-mehadrin.

sections.title: The Prohibition of Cheese of Non-Jews (Gevinat Akum)
sections.html:
In addition to the prohibition of milk of non-Jews, the Sages also forbade the cheese of non-Jews; that is, even if the milk is kosher, for example, because the non-Jew bought it from a Jew or because there is no impure animal anywhere in the area, the Sages decreed that the cheese he prepared is forbidden to eat. The Tanna'im and Amora'im gave many reasons for the decree, and from the fact that it was not clear what the reason for the decree was, one can learn that the general aim of the Sages in the decree on cheese, as in additional decrees on the foods of non-Jews, was to separate between Jews and non-Jews. In practice, however, they based their decree on the concern of a specific prohibition, upon which they established the sweeping prohibition on all cheeses. In halakha it was agreed that the main reason on which the prohibition of the cheese of non-Jews was founded is that non-Jews were accustomed to curdle the cheese with the stomach lining of a nevela (an animal not slaughtered properly) (Avoda Zara 29b; 35a-b).

To produce cheese from milk, one must mix into the milk enzymes (rennet) that break down the milk, separate the liquids and sugars from the proteins and fats, and bind the proteins and fats into a single mass, which is the cheese. Naturally, these enzymes are secreted in the stomach of mammals, to help them digest the milk they suckle. The food being digested in the stomach is called 'kiva' (rennet), whereas the stomach itself is called 'the stomach lining' (or ha-kiva). Jews would prepare cheeses using the 'kiva' of pure animals; that is, they used the contents of the stomach, in which these enzymes were present, to curdle the milk. Non-Jews, however, also used pieces of the stomach lining to curdle the milk. And since they did not slaughter the animals according to halakha, this lining was forbidden as nevela, and the cheeses curdled with it are forbidden to eat. And although the milk is much more than sixty times the stomach lining, since the cheese is curdled by it, the prohibition of nevela is not nullified in sixty, as its effect is evident in the cheese.

In recent generations the food industry has advanced, and today these enzymes are prepared from microorganisms. Still, there are places where stomach lining is used to make cheeses; this is done in less developed places, and it is done in developed countries when special cheeses with a tradition of generations are made.

The halakhic ruling is that even when it is known with certainty that the cheese that non-Jews prepared was made with enzymes that contain no prohibition, from plants or from microorganisms, their cheese is forbidden. This is because the decree of the Sages was enacted in a sweeping manner on all cheeses prepared by non-Jews.7

The poskim disagree whether the prohibition of cheese of non-Jews also applies to the liquid that remains from the milk after the cheese has curdled, which is called 'whey,' as explained in the note.8

sections.title: Permitted Ways for Non-Jews to Make Cheese
sections.html:
If the milk belongs to a Jew who hired the non-Jew as a worker to prepare cheese from it for him, according to many, as long as it is clear that there is no forbidden admixture in the cheese, the cheese is kosher. For the Sages forbade 'cheese of non-Jews,' meaning cheese that the non-Jew made from his own milk, and not cheese that he made from milk belonging to a Jew (Shakh 115:20; Pri Ḥadash 15; Noda Bi-Yehuda).

According to most poskim, just as when a Jew saw the non-Jew milking a pure animal, the milk milked under his supervision is kosher, so too, if a Jew saw that the non-Jew prepared cheese from kosher milk without adding the stomach lining of a nevela to it, the cheese is kosher (Rema 115:2; Minḥat Ya'akov; Noda Bi-Yehuda). And some say that even in this case the cheese is forbidden, and only if the Jew himself places the rennet in the milk to curdle it will the cheese be kosher (Shakh 20).9

sections.title: Soft Cheeses
sections.html:
The poskim disagree about the law of soft cheeses, such as white cheese, cottage cheese, leben and yogurt, which are formed by natural souring. That is, when milk is placed in a warm place, naturally, through the bacteria in the milk, the milk sours and becomes thick. In the first stage it becomes leben, and after some time it thickens into a soft cheese. To speed up the process of their formation, leftovers of leben or cheese that soured, which contain bacterial cultures, are added; different kinds of starters produce different dairy products, all of which have in common that they did not harden like cheese through enzymes but rather thickened through bacterial souring. Today, various concentrates of select bacteria are grown in advanced laboratories, which sour the milk precisely according to the desired product, and in this way dairy products are produced with a precise texture and taste.

Some permit the soft cheeses of non-Jews, because the decree on cheese is due to the concern that it is curdled with the stomach lining of a nevela, and consequently it applies only to cheeses curdled by means of enzymes found in the stomach; but soft cheeses, which are not curdled by enzymes but by bacteria, are permitted because they are not included in the prohibition.

However, according to most poskim, even if we say that the Sages decreed a prohibition on the cheese of non-Jews out of concern that they curdled it with enzymes of the stomach lining of a nevela, the decree applies to all dairy products that have thickened. In addition, some say that cheese was forbidden also out of concern that impure milk was mixed into the pure milk, and the softer the cheese, the greater this concern.

As a matter of halakha, it is proper to be stringent in accordance with the opinion of most poskim, and those who wish to be lenient may do so. In practice, there are kashrut bodies abroad that are lenient and give certification to soft cheeses made by non-Jews, while supervising that they are made from kosher ingredients. And in the Land of Israel the practice follows the opinion of most poskim, not to give certification to soft cheeses of non-Jews.10

sections.title: Butter
sections.html:
Butter is formed from milk by churning, that is, agitating the milk in a circular motion in order to separate the fat particles from the milk into a fatty layer, which is kneaded, compressed and consolidated into butter. Since the time of the Ge'onim the customs have been divided: some forbade the butter of non-Jews and some permitted it.

The reason of those who forbid is the prohibition of milk of non-Jews, that is, the concern that the non-Jew mixed impure milk into his milk before deciding to make butter from it. And although impure milk does not consolidate into butter, there is concern that the moisture remaining on the butter is from the impure milk. And although the likelihood of this is very low, the prohibition remains in force, because the Sages wanted to distance Jews from the foods of non-Jews (the custom of the Land of Israel in the time of the Ge'onim, Ra'avad and Rashba; Noda Bi-Yehuda Tinyana YD 65-66; Tzemaḥ Tzedek of Lubavitch YD 75).

The reason of those who permit is that the prohibition of milk of non-Jews does not apply to butter, since impure milk does not consolidate into butter. And the reason they forbade the cheese of non-Jews even though impure milk does not curdle is that they were concerned that it was curdled with the stomach lining of a nevela; but butter, which does not require such curdling, is not forbidden (Pri Ḥadash and the Gra in explaining the Rambam).11

According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 3:16), if the butter is cooked until the remnants of the milky liquid evaporate, there is no longer reason for concern according to those who forbid, for if there were remnants of impure milk on the butter, in the cooking they would evaporate or be completely nullified in the butter. And this is the opinion of most poskim (SA and Rema 115:3).

However, sometimes, for various reasons, the rabbis forbade butter. For example, in places where non-Jews cooked the butter in vessels that contained remnants of forbidden foods (Issur Ve-heter He-arokh 48:3), places where they mixed impure milk of a female camel into the butter (Pri To'ar 115:8), and places where they mixed forbidden fat (ḥelev) or lard into the butter (Ḥokhmat Adam 67:9; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 115:27).

In practice, as long as it is clear that the butter contains no forbidden ingredients, it is permitted, for the rule in a dispute concerning rabbinic law is that the halakha follows the lenient opinion, all the more so when this is the opinion of most poskim. And so most kashrut bodies practice, permitting the butter of non-Jews after checking that all the ingredients from which it is made are kosher. Those who are scrupulous take care to buy butter that was produced by Jews or whose production a Jew supervised.

sections.title: Milk Milked Forbiddenly on Shabbat
sections.html:
Milking on Shabbat is forbidden by Torah law (Shabbat 95a). However, to prevent suffering to the cows, for if they are not milked they will suffer greatly, it is permitted to ask a non-Jew to milk them. And although the Sages forbade a Jew to ask a non-Jew to do melakha for him on Shabbat, because of 'the suffering of animals' (tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim) the Sages set aside their own enactment. That milk is muktzeh for the whole of that Shabbat, and after Shabbat it is permitted to drink it or sell it (SA OḤ 305:20). Today the dairy industry has advanced, and milking is done by a pumping machine, and on Shabbat one should milk by means of 'gerama' (indirect causation). That is, the 'gerama' mechanism of the machine is activated on Friday, and on Shabbat a Jew attaches the milking cups to the cows' udders by vacuum, and this attachment causes the machine to begin pumping after a short time. This 'gerama' is permitted in order to prevent suffering to the cows, and after Shabbat it is permitted to benefit from the milk, since it was milked in a permitted manner. It is also possible to ask a non-Jew to milk on Shabbat using the pumping machine in the way one milks on a weekday, and after Shabbat it will be permitted to benefit from the milk (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 20:4).

But if the milk was milked by a Jew in desecration of Shabbat, by rabbinic law the milk is forbidden to the milker and to anyone for whom it was milked, so that they do not benefit from something done in desecration of Shabbat. And when it is milk intended to be marketed to the general public, it is forbidden to the entire public. In practice, however, since milk milked in desecration of Shabbat is mixed with milk milked on other days and with milk milked on Shabbat by a non-Jew, regarding any milk that reaches the store there is a doubt whether it was milked in a forbidden manner; and since the prohibition of benefiting from something done in desecration of Shabbat is rabbinic, in a situation of doubt there is no prohibition, and kashrut certification may be given to milk and dairy products that may contain milk milked in desecration of Shabbat. However, one should prefer milk from farms where Shabbat observance is maintained, both because it is kosher without doubt, and because it is proper to encourage Shabbat observance and so as not to assist in the desecration of Shabbat (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 26:7). Therefore, 'mehadrin' kashrut should not be given to dairy products that contain milk milked in desecration of Shabbat.

sections.title: Human Milk
sections.html:
A woman's milk, whether she is Jewish or not Jewish, is permitted to eat, provided that the milk has separated from her, for example, if she pumped it into a vessel. And it is not considered milk with respect to the prohibition of meat and milk.

But the Sages forbade suckling milk from a woman, and only an infant is permitted to suckle milk from his mother or from another wet nurse until he reaches the age of twenty-four months. After he reaches this age, if the child continues to nurse continuously, it is permitted to nurse him until the age of four, and if he is weak, until the age of five. But if he stopped nursing for three days (72 hours), and this interruption was not because he was sick, it is forbidden to nurse him, and his law is like that of any person: he is permitted to consume the milk after it has been pumped, but he is forbidden to suckle from the breast itself (Ketubot 60a; SA YD 81:7).12
